analysis.one_liner: Lets people sickened by glyphosate or elemental phosphorus exposure sue manufacturers and strips their federal immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has seen no hearing or vote; its sponsor and all six cosponsors are Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill does two things. First, it bars any federal money from carrying out Executive Order 14387, which directs the government to promote domestic production of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicides under the Defense Production Act. Second, it creates a federal right to sue: anyone injured by exposure to these chemicals can seek compensatory and punitive damages in federal court, and it explicitly nullifies the legal immunity that manufacturers would otherwise claim under the Defense Production Act or as federal contractors. It applies to past, current, and future claims and leaves state-law lawsuits untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to glyphosate herbicides or elemental phosphorus who developed an illness such as cancer, plus survivors and estates of those who died. The bill gives them a federal courtroom route to compensation that currently depends on state law, and it removes the defense that a company was just following a federal order. Farmworkers, agricultural workers, and people living near manufacturing sites are the most exposed groups.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmworkers and people exposed to glyphosate

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action for anyone who suffers injury, illness, disease, or death caused in whole or in part by exposure to elemental phosphorus or a glyphosate-based herbicide, with jurisdiction in federal district court regardless of the amount in controversy.
Authorizes compensatory damages (medical expenses, lost income, pain and suffering, wrongful death), punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees.
Waives and nullifies immunity under section 707 of the Defense Production Act and bars companies from using federal-contractor immunity or compliance with an executive order as a defense.
Prohibits any federal funds from being used to implement or enforce Executive Order 14387, which promotes phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicide production as a defense matter.
Applies to claims arising before, on, or after enactment and expressly preserves pending lawsuits and state-law remedies without preempting them.

analysis.who_pays: Glyphosate herbicide and elemental phosphorus manufacturers, which lose the legal immunity the executive order would provide and face compensatory and punitive damages in exposure lawsuits. Some cost could reach consumers and farmers through product prices if litigation risk is priced in.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to claims arising before enactment, exposing manufacturers to new liability for long-completed conduct; a company that complied with a federal defense-production order would still face damages, and defenders of the executive order argue that penalizing compliance deters companies from stepping in when the government asks.

The bill creates a route to damages without restricting the sale or use of glyphosate, so exposure could continue while liability accumulates, and it leaves unresolved the underlying scientific and regulatory dispute over how dangerous glyphosate is at typical exposure levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who believe their cancer or other illness came from these chemicals, the bill offers a meaningful new path to compensation, including punitive damages and fees, which ordinary plaintiffs rarely afford on their own. The main cost falls on manufacturers rather than taxpayers, though the retroactive reach and the elimination of the contractor-compliance defense go beyond typical products-liability rules and could be challenged as unfair to companies acting under federal direction. Notably, the bill does not limit glyphosate use itself, so it addresses compensation rather than prevention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, and it has stayed there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Martin Heinrich introduced S. 4425, the No Immunity for Glyphosate Act, on April 28, 2026, joined by Sens. Booker, Markey, Merkley, and Welch as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; the full action history shows no further action since then.
Six senators, all Democrats, are listed as cosponsors.
The bill targets Executive Order 14387 (91 Fed. Reg. 8703), which promotes an adequate defense supply of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicides, and would defund it.
The bill would strip manufacturers of immunity under Defense Production Act section 707 and bar any federal-contractor or compliance defense in exposure lawsuits, and it applies retroactively.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, for now: the executive order the bill targets remains in effect and the manufacturers' legal immunity has not been nullified, while people with exposure-related injuries still have only the lawsuits available to them under existing state law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, so far

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and took it to the Senate floor for introduction and referral.

against.name: President Trump
against.what_they_did: Issued Executive Order 14387 promoting national-defense supply of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate-based herbicides, the order this bill would defund and whose related legal immunity it would strip.

against.name: Sen. Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any committee hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican support is listed; the bill sits in a committee run by a Republican chair with no action scheduled.

industries.note: The bill would strip the legal immunity the executive order would provide and open these companies to compensatory and punitive damages from people claiming exposure-related injuries. Glyphosate is the most widely used weed killer in U.S. agriculture, and the largest maker has faced a large volume of cancer lawsuits for years, so the liability exposure is substantial.

The bill puts phosphorus in the same category as glyphosate for both the funding prohibition and the new right to sue, so producers lose the Defense Production Act protections the executive order would supply.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, but the bill has no Republican cosponsors, no committee action, and a Republican-controlled Senate calendar. The realistic path is that it dies in committee at the end of the Congress unless its provisions are folded into a larger, must-pass bill, which is uncommon for standalone liability bills like this one.
